segments.script: What covers your skin, lines your mouth, and can stretch to hold a full urinary bladder? Three types of compound epithelium — all built for protection and stress.
segments.video_prompt: Split-screen: left shows skin epidermis histology (striated layers, keratinised top). Right shows an animated empty vs. filled urinary bladder cross-section. Both panels dissolve into a title: 'Compound Epithelium'. Cinematic colour-graded biology style.

segments.script: Compound epithelium has many layers; only the innermost layer touches the basement membrane. Stratified squamous non-keratinised is in moist surfaces — mouth, oesophagus, vagina. Keratinised is in skin and all keratin derivatives: fish scales, reptile scutes, bird feathers, mammal hair, nail, horn, hoof. Keratin is a scleroprotein — hard, insoluble, waterproof. Stratified cuboidal is rare, in salivary and sweat gland ducts. Stratified columnar in conjunctiva and pharynx. Transitional epithelium or urothelium — relaxed cells are rounded; stretched cells flatten to squamous. Basement membrane visible when relaxed, invisible when stretched. Lines the urinary tract for high expansion.
segments.video_prompt: Left panel: comparison diagram of non-keratinised (smooth pink free border) vs. keratinised skin (rough cornified outer layer). Centre: collage of keratin derivatives in phylogenetic order — fish scales, reptile scutes, bird feathers, mammal nail. Right panel: transitional epithelium morphing animation — empty bladder with dome-shaped cells → filled bladder with flat squamous cells, baseline membrane appearing/disappearing. Smooth tween animation, clinical blue and white palette.
